newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian advance unit to reach Albania on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Italian advance unit to reach Albania on Friday.

text.p: An advance unit of Italian troops was setting out on Thursday for anarchic Albania to pave the way for a 6,000-strong multinational force amid doubts over the risks it could face and criticism of how it has been organised.

The troops, about 20 men from an Italian army pioneer regiment and a number of crack marines, were leaving the southeast port of Brindisi later in the day aboard a transport ship bound for the Albanian port of Durres across the Adriatic.
The Italian news agencies ANSA and AGI said the group, the first active soldiers from the force to land, would reach Durres on Friday morning and deploy with two armoured vehicles.
"Their task will be to inspect the area where the successive large landing will take place and inspect the state of the road that leads from Durres to Tirana," ANSA said.

The Defence Ministry would not discuss details but a spokesman confirmed that some men were scheduled to leave Italy by sea on Thursday. Military experts were also meeting in Rome to finalise plans for the large scale deployment.

The bulk of the force, the first of its kind led by Italy, is due to begin deploying next Monday on a mission to assist the delivery of relief aid to impoverished Albania, brought to the brink of collapse by an armed insurrection last month.

Comprised of troops from France, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Romania as well as Italy, it has U.N. Security Council approval but is being organised by a so-called "coalition of willing" nations. Austria and Denmark are also considering participation.

Italy had initially suggested Portugal would contribute but the country's Defence Minister Antonio Vitorino was quoted on Thursday as saying no soldiers would go because the conditions were not right and the risks were too great.

"This is essentially an internal, civil, guerrilla-style conflict. And so there should be an acceptance of this foreign military intervention by those for whom aid is intended," Vitorino told Publico newspaper.
"I have not seen the necessary willingness of the Albanians to accept such a mission," he said. "I believe it is a highly risky mission, and I have doubts it can reach its military objective."
Criticism also came from the European Parliament, which said the European Union's 15 member states had failed to act together to tackle the Albanian crisis.
Euro-deputies complained that by leaving Italy to shoulder the main burden, other EU governments were putting Rome under serious domestic pressure.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi won support late on Wednesday to send Italian troops to Albania but at the cost of a rift with his hard left allies that almost toppled his government.

The troops plan to secure Durres and the southern port of Vlore, the latter controlled by rebels, as well as Tirana airport and transport routes to protect food and medical aid. Prodi says they may have to stay for up to six months.
More than 200 people have been killed since rebels took control of the south last month in an eruption of anger following the collapse of shady get-rich-quick savings schemes.
Thousands of small arms looted from abandoned weapons depots are still on the streets and the Italian-led force has no mandate to take them out of circulation.
Albanian President Sali Berisha was quoted on Thursday as saying the risks to the force were minimal, comparing them with those faced by soldiers on manoeuvres.
